Right: three miniature copies, each highlighting one maximal clique in the accent color, listed beside it: [2, 3, 5], [3, 4], and [1, 2]." width="100%"} A clique is a subset of nodes where every pair of nodes is connected by an edge. A maximal clique is a clique that cannot be extended by adding another node. Uses the Bron-Kerbosch algorithm for efficient enumeration. Note that this finds *maximal* cliques (cannot be extended), not necessarily *maximum* cliques (largest possible). Use `maximum_clique()` to find a maximum clique. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [list[list[int]]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : List of cliques, where each clique is a sorted list of node IDs. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If called on a directed graph. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} Enumeration uses the Bron-Kerbosch algorithm with pivoting, whose worst-case runtime is $O(3^{n/3})$: the Moon-Moser theorem shows a graph on $n$ vertices can have that many maximal cliques, so the bound is tight. In practice most graphs stay far from the worst case and enumeration is fast. Note that *maximal* is a strictly weaker property than *maximum*: a clique is maximal if it cannot be extended by adding any vertex, but a graph may contain multiple maximal cliques of different sizes. Use `maximum_clique()` when you specifically want the largest one. Undirected graphs only; results come back with each clique's node IDs sorted, but the cliques themselves are in arbitrary order. ## Examples {.doc-examples} A triangle is itself one maximal clique containing all three nodes: ::: {#da159ac5 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ( ec.Graph(directed=False) .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C"]) .add_edges([("A", "B"), ("B", "C"), ("C", "A")]) ) cliques = graph.find_cliques() len(cliques) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 1 ``` ::: ::: ::: {#9ae61d88 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} len(cliques[0]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` 3 ``` ::: ::: A path graph instead has one clique per edge, since no three nodes are all mutually connected: ::: {#055cd53b .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ( ec.Graph(directed=False) .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D"]) .add_edges([("A", "B"), ("B", "C"), ("C", "D")]) ) len(graph.find_cliques()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` 3 ``` ::: ::: A complete graph collapses down to a single clique containing every node: ::: {#8bfbda03 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ec.Graph(directed=False) graph.add_full_graph(n=5) cliques = graph.find_cliques() len(cliques), len(cliques[0]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` (1, 5) ``` ::: :::
